One-sentence assessment: postsecondary chemistry teachers do more than "finish delivering a class": they organize courses and instruction around the chemical and physical properties and compositional changes of substances and combine teaching with research. The official scope is "Teach courses pertaining to the chemical and physical properties and compositional changes of substances. Work may include providing instruction in the methods of qualitative and quantitative chemical analysis. Includes both teachers primarily engaged in teaching, and those who do a combination of teaching and research". Daily work involves preparing and delivering undergraduate or graduate courses on topics such as organic chemistry, analytical chemistry and chemical separation (importance 94); establishing, teaching and monitoring students' compliance with safety rules for chemicals, equipment and other hazardous materials (93); evaluating and grading students' class work, laboratory performance, assignments and papers (89); supervising students' laboratory work (88); maintaining attendance, grades and other required records (86); supervising undergraduate or graduate teaching, internships and research (86); preparing, administering and grading examinations or assigning this work to others (84); preparing course materials such as syllabi, assignments and handouts (84); planning, evaluating and revising curricula, course content, materials and teaching methods (84); maintaining regular office hours to advise students (80); conducting research in a particular field and publishing findings in professional journals, books or electronic media (77); initiating, facilitating and moderating classroom discussions (76); keeping up with developments through reading literature, discussing with colleagues and attending professional conferences (73); advising students on academic and vocational curricula and career issues (69); and writing grant proposals to obtain external research funding (69). Other tasks include selecting, ordering and maintaining teaching and research materials and supplies (68), collaborating with colleagues on teaching and research issues (66), writing recommendation letters for students (65), preparing and submitting required teaching reports (64), serving on academic or administrative committees (64), cleaning laboratory facilities (59), participating in student recruitment, registration and placement (59), and serving on committees or professional associations (55), as well as administrative duties such as department head (supplemental 67), campus and community activities (supplemental 48), advising student organizations (supplemental 45), compiling specialized bibliographies for outside reading assignments (supplemental 44), and professional consulting for government or industry (supplemental 38). O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone Five (extensive preparation), with SVP 8.0 and above and interest code IS (Investigative, Social); BLS shows that most positions require graduate education, many require a doctoral degree, a master's degree may suffice at community colleges and similar positions, and some require work experience in the field. The core boundary: this academic position centers on course teaching and student guidance and may include research, rather than primarily process development engineering; this page does not present mainland Chinese postsecondary teacher qualifications and appointment conditions as uniform thresholds or U.S. education and tenure systems as universal institutions.

Signals for further exploration: you are willing to move between classrooms and laboratories over the long term, explain complex concepts clearly, and turn processes and requirements into checkable records. O*NET work context shows 98% of respondents use email daily, 88% work indoors in environmentally controlled conditions daily, 82% have face-to-face discussions daily, 83% typically work more than 40 hours per week, 79% have substantial freedom in making decisions (18% some freedom), 79% have substantial freedom in determining tasks and priorities, 52% have contact with others most of the time (22% about half the time), 50% consider being exact or accurate extremely important, 39% very important, 48% bear very high responsibility for others' health and safety, 29% high responsibility, 49% very high responsibility for others' work outcomes, 45% consider teamwork extremely important, 46% speak publicly daily, 37% sit continually or almost continually, 34% consider competition extremely intense, 34% highly competitive, and 27% face time pressure daily; 68% report completely unautomated work, 18% slightly automated work, and 92% regular schedules. These figures indicate substantial time spent preparing and teaching courses, advising and documenting, real grading and safety responsibilities, and considerable autonomy and scheduling flexibility.

Conditions for pausing substantial investment: you have not completed a supervised practice cycle of "understand course goals and the education program → design a lesson and experiment → teach and organize discussion → grade assignments and laboratory reports → handle academic integrity and safety issues → record grades and propose improvements"; you are unwilling to face public speaking and ongoing grading; or you tend to appease rather than follow policy when students violate safety rules or academic integrity. Do not underestimate teaching workloads just because you "like chemistry": the core tasks are preparing and teaching courses and establishing and monitoring safety compliance. If you prefer long-term laboratory research and publication without systematic teaching responsibility, chemists and biochemists are adjacent positions with different requirements.

Check education, qualifications and authorization separately: O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone Five (extensive preparation), with SVP 8.0 and above; BLS shows most positions require graduate education, many require doctoral degrees, master's degrees may suffice at community colleges and similar positions, and some require field work experience. This occupation's O*NET certification page lists 2 national certifications (National Board Certification - Science - Adolescence and Young Adulthood; LIUNA Instructor Certification), with no registered apprenticeship occupations listed at that time. Industry certifications are capability credentials and employer preferences, rather than postsecondary appointment qualifications or tenure. In the United States, appointments and promotion are determined by institutional policies and departmental review, without a uniform national teacher license; in mainland China, postsecondary teaching positions involve public institution recruitment, higher education teacher qualifications and professional title reviews, to be checked against local and institutional rules. This page does not extend one jurisdiction's requirements to others. Education and training, industry certification, statutory and position qualifications, and institutional appointment and authorization are four different matters.

In one sentence: this position turns "whether course goals were achieved, students truly mastered the material, laboratory and chemical safety was maintained, grading and records withstand review, and research outputs can be examined by peers" into reviewable evidence. Outputs include syllabi and course materials, teaching and seminar records, laboratory and safety procedures and student safety training records, grading criteria and grade and feedback records, academic integrity handling records, advising and research meeting records, papers, patents, grant proposals and funding records, and committee and academic service records. This is more than an experimental operations position and does not replace institutional academic administration and academic committees' final determinations on grade recognition, degrees, appointments and academic misconduct.

The following three work areas summarize O*NET tasks; actual workloads depend on institutions and appointment tracks. Postsecondary chemistry teachers' work can be divided into three connected but distinct areas. First, teaching and courses: prepare materials and syllabi, teach organic chemistry, analytical chemistry and related courses, initiate and moderate discussions, prepare and grade examinations, and evaluate and revise curricula. Second, laboratories and safety: supervise students' laboratory work, establish and teach safety rules for chemicals, equipment and hazardous materials and monitor compliance, select, order and maintain laboratory materials and supplies, and maintain facilities. Third, research, advising and academic service: conduct and publish research, write funding proposals, advise graduate students and theses, maintain office hours and write recommendations, and participate in departmental and academic committees and professional associations. Teachers have teaching, grading and advising responsibilities; teaching evaluation, academic misconduct investigation and handling, and safety management follow divisions of responsibility by policy and jurisdiction, rather than all being decided by committees.
Design and teach courses and organize discussion and assessment according to course goals

Read the education program, prerequisites and course goals → write syllabi, materials and grading criteria → prepare teaching content, classroom activities and laboratory arrangements → teach, organize discussion and observe students' understanding → prepare and grade assessments in line with criteria → provide feedback and record grades and teaching improvements
Organize laboratory teaching according to safety procedures and supervise students' experimental operations

Editorial checking workflow: check experiments, hazards and risk assessments → implement institutional access, training, assessment and protection conditions → prepare reagents and equipment according to procedures and check safety facilities → supervise operations; promptly stop dangerous behavior, report or seek help under emergency policies → retain teaching and safety records. China's Safety Specifications for Higher Education Laboratories apply to teaching, research, experiments and practical training in higher education; Article 7 separately identifies laboratory heads and project leads (including course instructors) as directly responsible persons and persons with primary responsibility for project safety. Pre-experiment training and assessment, hazard identification and project risk assessments must be implemented; activities cannot proceed while major hazards remain unresolved. Article 2 of the 2024 grading and classification measures explicitly excludes pilot and industrial scale-up sites, which must not be generalized.

Grade assignments, laboratory reports and examinations according to previously published criteria and explain the reasons; maintain traceable attendance and grade records; collect evidence and report suspected plagiarism or data fabrication according to policy; immediately stop unsafe experimental behavior and handle it under safety policies. Do not change grades or records without verification or substitute personal impressions for grading evidence.

Common adjacent positions include chemists, biochemists and biophysicists, molecular and cellular biologists, natural sciences managers, biomedical engineers and postsecondary physics teachers. Boundaries depend on "who bears systematic course teaching and student advising responsibilities, who is responsible for research outputs, funding and teams, and who has authority to determine grades, safety and academic standards", rather than titles.

Central outputs are courses, teaching outcomes, student development and reviewable teaching and research records
Based on education programs, course goals, grading criteria, safety procedures and academic standards

Chemists may also perform analytical testing, quality control and product and method development; this occupation's identity centers on teaching chemistry and advising students in higher education, either primarily teaching or combining teaching with research.
Prepare and teach courses, organize discussions and laboratory instruction, grade and provide feedback, hold office hours and advise, conduct and publish research, and provide academic service

Chemists may undertake research and analysis in R&D, testing and manufacturing; the two occupations may share experimental skills, but ongoing course teaching responsibilities require checking the actual position.
Syllabi and course materials, grade and feedback records, laboratory safety and training records, and publication, project and funding records

Biochemists and molecular and cellular biologists may also teach and advise students; the main differences concern research objects and training in living systems, rather than an absolute research/teaching divide.

Course instructors are responsible for teaching, academic assessment and grade records; grade reviews follow institutional procedures. Degree awards, appointments and academic misconduct investigations and handling involve other responsible bodies and policies; daily grading cannot all be assigned to committees.

U.S. BLS table 1.2 lists typical entry education as a doctoral or professional degree; the broader OOH description says four-year institutions generally require doctorates, while some fields, part-time positions and community colleges accept master's degrees. Articles 10–13 of China's Teachers Law and Articles 4, 6–8 and 12–16 of the Regulations on Teacher Qualifications distinguish education conditions, examination applicability and recognition for higher education teacher qualifications: the statutory education condition is graduation with graduate or undergraduate education, but other conditions and lawful recognition remain necessary. This differs from institutional recruitment requirements for doctorates, research outputs and appointment conditions; not all applicants follow the same training and examination procedure. Six recurring occupational judgments: whether course goals align with assessments; whether laboratory safety rules are actually followed; whether students' difficulties concern understanding or foundations; whether grading evidence is consistent and reviewable; whether academic integrity issues follow policy; and how to allocate research and teaching time.
Judgment one: do course goals align with assessments?

First confirm whether assessment content and formats cover the knowledge and abilities required by course goals, then decide question difficulty and weights; do not distinguish students using irrelevant or out-of-syllabus content or use participation as the sole grading basis.
Judgment two: are laboratory safety rules actually followed?

Before experiments in Chinese higher education institutions, complete safety training and assessment according to policy, rather than only oral awareness; continuously supervise protection, ventilation and waste operations, promptly stopping and reporting violations. Select protection and responses according to project risk assessments, institutional procedures and actual emergency duties.
Judgment three: do difficulties concern understanding or foundations?

When grades are anomalous or classroom responses are slow, first check prerequisite knowledge, then adjust teaching or strengthen foundations; rule out course design and explanation problems before attributing teaching difficulties to student ability.
Judgment four: is grading evidence consistent and reviewable?

Publish criteria before assessment and apply them consistently to similar answers; comments should cite specific evidence so students and reviewers can understand, and original answers and grading records should be retained for disputed grades.
Judgment five: do academic integrity issues follow policy?

Check suspected ordinary assignment cheating against school assessment and student management rules; for academic misconduct in research and related activities in China, the institution accepts cases under Ministry of Education Order 40, the academic committee organizes investigation and findings, and the institution handles cases according to procedure. Retain leads, report according to duties, and protect opportunities for statements and defenses and confidentiality, rather than publicly declaring guilt as a teacher.
Judgment six: how should research and teaching time be allocated?

Allocate time according to institution type and appointment requirements: research universities generally place greater demands on research outputs, while teaching institutions and community colleges emphasize teaching and student services. Turn annual goals into checkable task lists instead of balancing by intuition.

Postsecondary chemistry teachers teach courses on the chemical and physical properties and compositional changes of substances, which may include methods of qualitative and quantitative chemical analysis; some primarily teach and others combine teaching with research (official O*NET-SOC 25-1052.00 scope). Daily work involves preparing and delivering undergraduate or graduate courses on organic chemistry, analytical chemistry and chemical separation; establishing, teaching and monitoring compliance with safety rules for chemicals, equipment and other hazardous materials; evaluating and grading class work, laboratory performance, assignments and papers; supervising laboratory work; maintaining attendance, grades and other required records; supervising undergraduate or graduate teaching, internships and research; preparing, administering and grading examinations or assigning this work to others; preparing syllabi, assignments and handouts; planning, evaluating and revising curricula, course content, materials and teaching methods; maintaining regular office hours; conducting and publishing research in professional journals, books or electronic media; initiating, facilitating and moderating discussions; keeping up with developments through literature, colleagues and conferences; advising on academic and vocational curricula and career issues; writing external funding proposals; selecting, ordering and maintaining teaching and research materials and supplies; collaborating on teaching and research issues; writing recommendations; preparing required teaching reports; serving on academic or administrative committees addressing institutional policy, departmental matters and academic issues; cleaning laboratories; participating in student recruitment, registration and placement; serving on committees or professional associations; and possibly undertaking administrative duties such as department head, joining campus and community activities, advising student organizations, compiling specialized bibliographies, or consulting for government and industry. Responsibility boundaries: instructors have teaching, academic assessment and recordkeeping duties; in China, project leads (including course instructors) implement project laboratory safety responsibilities. Check degrees, appointments, research academic misconduct and accident handling against the applicable responsible bodies and procedures; not all grade or safety responsibilities belong to committees.

The six directions share some capabilities with this occupation: systematic subject knowledge, data analysis and writing, project and time management, and collaboration. The actual differences concern objects (courses and students or research and products), assessment (teaching quality and student development or publications, projects and business metrics), and responsibilities (teaching and grading or research conclusions and product validation). First test yourself with deliverable teaching or research materials instead of comparing titles.

Comparisons are based on task and work activity descriptions on the O*NET-SOC 25-1052.00 page, the adjacent occupation list registered in this evidence route (natural-sciences-managers, biomedical-engineers, biochemists-and-biophysicists, molecular-and-cellular-biologists, chemists), and editorial position boundary explanations. Check entry, appointment and authorization requirements separately against each position's own page and employer policies; this table establishes no statutory duties or qualification rules.

The table compares adjacent positions and occupations: chemists, biochemists and biophysicists, molecular and cellular biologists, natural sciences managers, biomedical engineers and postsecondary physics teachers. Its four columns address the same kinds of questions: what each direction does, its key difference from this occupation, and who is better suited to choose it.

Chemists are primarily assessed on research outputs and generally do not bear systematic course teaching and student development responsibilities; this occupation centers on course teaching and advising, with research as a parallel task.
People seeking long-term laboratory research and outputs suit chemist work; people seeking to turn knowledge into courses and take responsibility for student development suit this occupation.
Conduct chemical research in research institutions or company laboratories, with research reports, publications and patents as the main outputs.
Chemists

Biochemists and biophysicists focus on molecular mechanisms in living systems and more specialized research questions; this occupation's courses cover broader chemical topics such as chemical foundations, analytical chemistry and chemical separation.
People seeking deep work on molecular mechanisms in life sciences suit biochemistry and biophysics; people wishing to teach foundational chemistry courses suit this occupation.
Study chemical and physical mechanisms of biomolecules and life processes, mainly producing research findings and methods.
Biochemists and Biophysicists
Molecular and cellular biologists' training and research objects lean toward biology; this occupation is grounded in chemistry and provides chemistry instruction.
People preferring biological questions and experimental techniques suit molecular and cellular biology; people preferring chemistry, substance properties and analytical methods suit this occupation.
Study biological questions at cellular and molecular levels in laboratories, mainly producing research findings and experimental methods.
Molecular and Cellular Biologists

Natural sciences managers organize work, allocate resources and manage performance, generally no longer teaching daily; this occupation's frontline duties are teaching and advising, with management usually temporary or concurrent.
People seeking team and resource management suit natural sciences management; people wishing to remain in frontline teaching and advising suit this occupation.
Manage research or production teams, budgets and projects, mainly producing team outcomes and business metrics.
Natural Sciences Managers
Biomedical engineers produce engineering devices and validation data and are assessed on products and projects; this occupation produces courses, student development and academic outputs.
People seeking device and product development suit biomedical engineering; people seeking teaching and academic research suit this occupation.
Apply engineering methods to develop and validate biomedical devices and materials, mainly producing devices and solutions.
Biomedical Engineers

Postsecondary physics teachers work with physical laws and experiments, with curricula and laboratory safety management differing from chemistry; this occupation teaches chemistry, substance properties and analytical chemistry.
People preferring physics and experiments suit postsecondary physics teaching; people preferring chemistry, analytical testing and safety management suit this occupation.
Teach physics courses and conduct physics research in higher education, mainly producing courses and research findings.
Physics Teachers, Postsecondary

If you prefer long-term research and outputs, compare chemists and biochemists and biophysicists; for team and resource management, compare natural sciences managers; for engineering and product development, compare biomedical engineers; for physics courses and experiments, compare postsecondary physics teachers. Their entry, appointment and assessment structures differ from this occupation; do not confuse this page's teaching and advising judgments with final authority over research or products.

entries.answer: Daily tasks mainly involve course teaching, student advising and research: prepare and deliver organic chemistry, analytical chemistry and chemical separation courses, prepare materials and syllabi, initiate and moderate discussions, prepare and grade examinations and evaluate and revise courses, supervise laboratory work and establish and monitor chemical and equipment safety rules, maintain office hours and advise academic and research work, and conduct and publish research. O*NET work context shows 98% use email daily, 82% have face-to-face discussions daily, 46% speak publicly daily, and 83% typically work more than 40 hours per week.
entries.question: What do postsecondary chemistry teachers do every day?

entries.answer: Chemists are primarily assessed on research outputs and generally do not teach systematically; natural sciences managers focus on teams, resources and projects and generally no longer teach daily; postsecondary physics teachers' subjects and experimental systems concern physics. This occupation centers on chemistry teaching and student development and may combine these with research.
entries.question: How does this position differ from chemists, natural sciences managers and postsecondary physics teachers?

entries.answer: Public materials do not support this conclusion. Core tasks center on course design and teaching, grading and feedback, laboratory safety supervision and academic advising; judging mastery, handling academic integrity and stopping laboratory violations require teachers responsible for people and safety. BLS projects growth 2% and 1,900 average annual openings for 2024–2034, representing employment size projections, rather than replacement rates.

entries.answer: Steps with structured inputs: materials and exercise drafts, organizing feedback text, compiling learning data, searching literature and organizing citations. Steps requiring on-site judgment and responsibility for people and safety are affected later.

entries.answer: Reading Comprehension, Speaking and Writing (O*NET basic skill importance each 78); Active Learning, Active Listening, Critical Thinking, Learning Strategies, Monitoring and Science (each 75); Complex Problem Solving and Instructing (each 72) have the highest transferable skill scores. Social orientation, achievement orientation, intellectual curiosity, integrity and dependability are key work styles.

entries.answer: O*NET places the occupation in Job Zone Five (extensive preparation), with SVP 8.0 and above; BLS shows most positions require graduate education, many require doctorates, master's degrees may suffice at community colleges and similar positions, and some require field work experience.
entries.question: What education is needed to enter the occupation?

entries.answer: U.S. postsecondary teachers have no uniform national teacher license; appointments and promotion follow institutional policies and departmental review. O*NET's certification page listed 2 national certifications (National Board Certification - Science; LIUNA Instructor Certification), representing capability credentials and employer preferences. In mainland China, teaching positions involve public institution recruitment, higher education teacher qualifications and professional title reviews; laboratory teaching and hazardous chemical management positions have additional laboratory safety management requirements.
entries.question: Are licenses or certifications required?

entries.answer: Switching from research institutions or company R&D generally requires building teaching capability and course design experience and adapting to public speaking and ongoing grading; switching from secondary school teaching requires greater subject depth and research capability. Specific recognition follows institutional policies; this page gives no uniform conclusion.
entries.question: Is switching from another position difficult?

entries.answer: This depends on your goals: if you want teaching and student development as core duties and accept appointment-period assessments and competitive evaluations, this pathway offers stable academic career development and considerable autonomy. However, BLS projects only 2% employment growth in 2024–2034 (slower than average for all occupations), and research positions have substantial output and funding demands, so consider institution type and subject differences. This page provides facts and boundaries, rather than personal decisions.
